section_summary: This section records the 1938 dispute over whether American citizens in Japan were exempt from special taxes connected with Japan’s military operations in China under the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. It includes American and British diplomatic notes, Japanese replies, legal analysis, telegrams, and records of a July conversation. Britain ultimately declined to pursue a further rejoinder, while the United States reaffirmed its objection.

people.name: F. X. Ward
people.role: Author of a State Department legal memorandum

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 154 concerning Japan’s reply on special taxes
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s refusal to exempt American citizens and requests authority for a rejoinder and consular advice.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages quote Japan’s argument that the taxes are ordinary revenues and not military exactions under the 1911 treaty. Grew proposes further diplomatic discussion and advice that Americans refrain from payment, paying under protest if threatened with distraint.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 158 suggesting a rejoinder
subfiles.about: Suggests arguments against Japan’s tax position and reports a forthcoming British protest.
subfiles.summary: Grew argues that the taxes support hostilities in China regardless of how they are legislated or accounted for. He proposes invoking Britain’s current agreement that its nationals should be exempt.

subfiles.title: Department telegram No. 98 authorizing a rejoinder
subfiles.about: Authorizes Grew’s rejoinder and instructions to the Consul General.
subfiles.summary: The Department directs Grew to emphasize both the military special account and the treaty exemption for taxes supporting hostilities in China.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting British note on special taxes
subfiles.about: Quotes the British request to end collection of the special taxes from British nationals.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Britain regards the taxes as military contributions prohibited by its treaty with Japan.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file note on despatch No. 2796
subfiles.about: Records that the despatch’s substance had already been telegraphed and acted upon.
subfiles.summary: No further action is indicated.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2796 transmitting American aide-mémoire
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Embassy’s February 21 protest against Japanese military taxes on Americans.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses the aide-mémoire delivered to the Japanese Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: American aide-mémoire on exemption from Japanese military taxes
subfiles.about: Asserts that American citizens and corporations are exempt from taxes earmarked for military operations.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy cites the special military expenditure account and Article I of the 1911 treaty, and asks Japan to stop collecting the taxes from Americans.

subfiles.title: Legal memorandum comparing American and Japanese war taxes
subfiles.about: Assesses whether the United States War Revenue Act weakens the treaty argument against Japan’s taxes.
subfiles.summary: Ward distinguishes American taxes paid into the general treasury from Japanese taxes allocated to a military expenditure account. He concludes that the Japanese taxes can reasonably be treated as military exactions under the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on despatch No. 2841
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the American and British notes enclosed with Grew’s despatch.
subfiles.summary: The note recommends reading the Embassy’s forceful reply and the parallel British note.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2841 transmitting notes on special taxes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the American rejoinder, Japan’s earlier note verbale, and a British note.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards the correspondence concerning treaty exemptions from Japan’s special taxes.

subfiles.title: American Ambassador’s note No. 899 to Hirota
subfiles.about: Rejects Japan’s interpretation of the special taxes and the treaty’s military-exactions clause.
subfiles.summary: Grew maintains that the special taxes finance military operations in China and that their legislative form does not remove the treaty exemption. He cites the Finance Minister’s explanation of the taxes and rejects Japan’s reliance on an earlier British position, observing that Britain currently shares the American objection.

subfiles.title: Japanese note verbale No. 27
subfiles.about: Rejects the American claim that special taxes are prohibited military contributions.
subfiles.summary: Japan says the taxes remain general revenues despite their transfer to a special account. It interprets military exactions as exceptional levies imposed by military authorities and refuses to discontinue collection from American residents.

subfiles.title: British Embassy covering card to Grew
subfiles.about: Sends the British Embassy’s compliments with its note.
subfiles.summary: Covering card accompanying the British diplomatic note.

subfiles.title: British Ambassador’s note to Hirota
subfiles.about: Requests exemption of British subjects from the North China Incident special taxes.
subfiles.summary: Craigie traces the tax revenues through the military expenditure account and argues that they constitute military contributions barred by the Anglo-Japanese treaty.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Grew’s June telegram
subfiles.about: Recommends awaiting Japan’s response to the American rejoinder.
subfiles.summary: The Division believes no immediate action is required.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 358 on Britain’s decision against a rejoinder
subfiles.about: Explains why Britain will not answer Japan’s refusal to exempt British subjects.
subfiles.summary: Craigie reports that Britain fears weakening its own ability to tax foreign residents during a future war. Grew has received no reply to the American rejoinder.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 387 reporting Japan’s reply
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s renewed refusal to exempt Americans from the special taxes.
subfiles.summary: Japan again defines military exactions as emergency levies imposed by military authorities.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2942 transmitting Japan’s reply to Britain
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Encloses Japan’s refusal to suspend collection of special taxes from British residents.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards Hirota’s April 18 reply to Craigie.

subfiles.title: Hirota’s note No. 48 to the British Ambassador
subfiles.about: Rejects Britain’s claim that the special taxes are exempt military contributions.
subfiles.summary: Hirota argues that the taxes fund general expenditure and retain their ordinary character despite accounting transfers. He distinguishes normal taxation from military requisitions, invokes the 1904 precedent, and refuses to suspend collection.

subfiles.title: Document file note for despatch No. 2910
subfiles.about: Cross-references Grew’s account of the notes exchanged over special taxes.
subfiles.summary: File note points to despatch No. 2910 on American payment of Japanese military taxes.

subfiles.title: Payment by American Citizens of Special Japanese Taxes for Military Expenditures in China
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Japanese and American notes exchanged in March 1938.
subfiles.summary: The account outlines Japan’s position that the taxes are ordinary revenues and the American reply that they support military operations and fall within the treaty exemption. It notes Britain’s agreement with the American position at that stage.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2990 transmitting Craigie’s confidential explanation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards Craigie’s explanation for declining a British rejoinder.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits Craigie’s confidential June 3 letter.

subfiles.title: Craigie’s confidential letter to Grew
subfiles.about: Explains Britain’s decision not to pursue its objection to the Japanese taxes.
subfiles.summary: Craigie says Britain wishes to preserve its ability to tax foreign residents in a future war. He also describes Britain’s limited 1904 position on Japanese consumption taxes.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3040 transmitting Japan’s second American reply
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Ugaki’s June 4 note and its explanation of Japan’s treaty position.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Japan continues to define military exactions as emergency assessments by military authorities and awaits further instructions.

subfiles.title: Ugaki’s note No. 60 to Grew
subfiles.about: States that Japan will not withdraw its position on taxing American residents.
subfiles.summary: Ugaki refers Grew to the separately stated reasons.

subfiles.title: Annex explaining Japan’s interpretation of military exactions
subfiles.about: Explains why Japan considers its special taxes outside the treaty exemption.
subfiles.summary: The annex defines military exactions as exceptional, direct assessments by military authorities in emergencies. It argues that taxes imposed through ordinary legal procedures remain ordinary taxes regardless of whether their proceeds support military purposes, and that resident foreigners must pay them.

subfiles.title: Department telegram No. 252 reaffirming treaty exemption
subfiles.about: Directs Grew to reaffirm the American objection to collecting the taxes.
subfiles.summary: The Department says collection would violate the reciprocal treaty exemption and that Americans should be informed if they inquire.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 480 reporting conversation with Ugaki
subfiles.about: Reports delivering the Department’s position to Ugaki.
subfiles.summary: Ugaki said he knew nothing about the subject and would investigate.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on despatch No. 3140
subfiles.about: Reviews the Embassy’s memorandum of its conversation with Ugaki.
subfiles.summary: The Division notes that Grew followed instructions and that no action is required.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3140 transmitting conversation memorandum
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Encloses Grew’s record of his July 21 conversation with Ugaki.
subfiles.summary: Grew confirms that he carried out the Department’s instructions orally.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Grew’s conversation with Ugaki
subfiles.about: Records Grew’s oral representation and Ugaki’s response.
subfiles.summary: Grew delivered a prepared statement; Ugaki said he would investigate.

subfiles.title: Grew’s statement to Ugaki on special taxes
subfiles.about: Reaffirms that collecting the taxes from Americans would violate the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The statement says Americans will be informed of the government’s position if collection is attempted.
